deities: Lord Rama (presiding deity; black stone idol, from which the temple takes its name)
Goddess Sita (black stone idol in the sanctum)
Lakshmana (black stone idol in the sanctum)
Lord Hanuman (black stone idol at the entrance)
festivals: Kumbh Mela (major gathering point during Nashik Kumbh)

history.dynasty: Maratha (Peshwa era); patron Sardar Rangrao Odhekar
history.summary: The Kalaram Mandir in Panchavati, Nashik, was built between 1788 and 1792 by Sardar Rangrao Odhekar, an official of the Peshwa administration of the Maratha Empire. Tradition says Odhekar dreamt of black idols of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana submerged in the Godavari; the idols were retrieved from the river and enshrined in the new temple, built entirely of black basalt stone - 'Kalaram' literally means 'black Rama', rare among Rama temples. Smaller shrines (Vithal, Ganapati, Maruti) and an ancient tree with Dattatreya's footprint mark surround the main shrine. The temple also has national social-historical significance: in 1930 Dr. B. R. Ambedkar led the Kalaram Satyagraha outside the temple demanding temple entry for Dalits, a landmark of India's social reform movement.

name: Kalaram Temple
town_description: Nashik, on the banks of the Godavari, is one of India's holiest cities and the host of the Kumbh Mela every 12 years. The Panchavati quarter, where the Kalaram Temple stands, is steeped in Ramayana lore - Sita's cave, Ramkund and the Godavari ghats all lie nearby. Nashik is also a fast-growing city famed for its wine industry (Sula Vineyards) and as a major onion and grape trade centre.

travel.railway: Nashik Road Railway Station (approx. 8-10 km; verify)
travel.road: In the Panchavati area of Nashik city, about 3-4 km from the central bus stand; easily reached by auto, taxi and city bus.

visitor_information.best_time: October-March for pleasant weather; Ram Navami and Dussehra are festive high points.
visitor_information.opening_hours: CONFLICT (verify): sources variously list 5:00/5:30 AM to 10:00 PM daily, or 6:00 AM-12:00 PM and 5:00-8:00 PM. Free entry; photography allowed in the courtyard but not inside the sanctum.
